papers.title: Quercetin alters redox homeostasis, induces MAPK activation and promotes DNA damage in vGPCR-transformed endothelial cells
papers.abstract: Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is an angioproliferative tumor associated with infection by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV). Among the viral genes involved in KS pathogenesis, the viral G protein-coupled receptor (vGPCR) plays a key role in oncogenic transformation and angiogenesis, and its sustained activity contributes to tumor development and maintenance. Quercetin (QUE), a naturally occurring flavonoid with well-recognized anticancer properties, has been shown to reduce cell viability and proliferation and to induce apoptosis in vGPCR-transformed endothelial cells. This study further investigated the mechanisms underlying the antineoplastic effects of QUE in vGPCR cells, an in vitro model of Kaposi's sarcoma. Initially, QUE promoted the activation of MAPK signaling pathways in vGPCR cells, increasing the phosphorylation levels of ERK1/2, JNK1/2, and p38, without affecting AKT phosphorylation. In parallel, QUE increased intracellular oxidant levels, followed by lipid peroxidation and DNA damage, supporting a link between oxidative imbalance and genotoxicity. However, increased total glutathione content, and unaltered Gpx4 mRNA expression, suggest the induction of oxidative stress and compensatory antioxidant responses. Furthermore, increased intracellular oxidant levels were associated with MAPK signaling activation, particularly JNK1/2, whereas ERK1/2 and p38 activation may reflect a compensatory response that is insufficient to overcome QUE-induced cytotoxicity. Taken together, these findings indicate that QUE exerts antiproliferative effects in vGPCR cells through a mechanism involving oxidative stress, MAPK activation, and DNA damage, supporting its potential relevance in the study of therapeutic strategies for virus-associated malignancies.

papers.title: Tracing the dynamic recruitment trajectory of Optineurin between the centrosome and other macromolecular assemblies, signifying its role in cell cycle progression
papers.abstract: Spatiotemporal allocation and dynamic redistribution of centrosomal proteins are critical for coordinating the structural and molecular events that ensure successful cell division. While depletion of the multifunctional protein Optineurin (OPTN) impairs cell-cycle progression, our previous report of the presence of OPTN at key cell-division assemblies raised the question of how its trafficking is coordinated during cell division. In this study, using cell-cycle synchronisation coupled with flow cytometric analysis and confocal microscopy, we report that OPTN progressively dissociates from centrosomes during mitosis, redistributes to cytokinetic structures, accumulates at the spindle midzone, and then concentrates at the midbody during cytokinesis. Moreover, following this transition, OPTN progressively re-emerges at centrosomes during G1 of the subsequent cell cycle. Further, microtubule perturbation and regrowth assays provide evidence that OPTN recruitment and retention at the pericentriolar matrix (PCM) can occur independently of microtubules, whereas its exit is microtubule-dependent. Collectively, this study depicts, for the first time, a detailed movement trail of OPTN, highlighting its centrosome-linked redistribution and microtubule dependency. This context-dependent localisation and trafficking of OPTN across the centrosome-midbody axis establish a definitive spatiotemporal roadmap that can be strategically utilised to study its functional role in cell division.

papers.title: Combined celecoxib and NDGA induces a non-canonical, autophagy-independent redox cell death via p62/KEAP1 in colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) exhibits substantial intratumoral heterogeneity, with differences in oncogenic driver mutations and apoptotic competence contributing to therapeutic resistance. Here, we investigated whether combined celecoxib and NDGA treatment (C+N) induces redox-mediated cell death via the p62/KEAP1 axis, offering a therapeutic approach that can overcome genetic diversity in CRC. We used two genetically distinct CRC cell lines, HCT116 and HT29, harbouring KRAS and BRAF mutations respectively, with differing p53 status, as models of tumor heterogeneity. C+N exhibited profound cytotoxicity in both cell lines, independent of COX-2/5-LOX expression and apoptotic competence. Additionally, C+N induced marked oxidative stress with mitochondrial ROS, lipid peroxidation, and labile ferrous iron accumulation, visualized as distinct JC-1 green mitochondrial puncta and FerroOrange red iron puncta in both cell lines. The antioxidant NAC reversed C+N-induced death, but inhibitors of apoptosis, autophagy, necroptosis, or ferroptosis did not, indicating a mechanism distinct from these pathways. Mechanistically, the combination induced p62 Ser349 phosphorylation, promoting KEAP1 degradation and NRF2 stabilization independently of ULK1-mediated autophagy; however, NRF2 stabilization was uncoupled from HO-1 induction. Our work reveals that C+N induces a ULK1/autophagy-independent, redox-mediated cell death mechanism that circumvents apoptotic competence, highlighting redox disruption as a genotype-independent therapeutic strategy to overcome CRC heterogeneity.

papers.title: The Gαi/o GPCR LPAR2 Acts as a Non-Classical Factor for Aldosterone Induced Injury in a Cardiomyocyte Model
papers.abstract: Aldosterone is a key regulator of systemic sodium, potassium, and fluid homeostasis. Chronic elevation of aldosterone, as observed in primary aldosteronism, chronic heart and kidney diseases, promotes cardiac hypertrophy, inflammation, fibrosis, and heart failure, which are further enhanced in aging. Although these pathological effects are primarily attributed to the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR), emerging evidence suggests roles for nonclassical G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling. We identified lysophosphatidic acid receptor 2 (LPAR2) as a novel GPCR candidate that mediates aldosterone signaling in cardiomyocytes. Using AC16 human cardiomyocyte cells and reporter gene assays, we demonstrate that aldosterone activates a Gi/o-dependent GPCR pathway. Pharmacological inhibition of LPAR2 internalization confirms its specific reaction to aldosterone. Functional studies revealed that aldosterone-induced cardiomyocyte injury requires both MR and LPAR2, where specific antagonists to both receptors reduced the ability of aldosterone to induce collagen expression and cell death markers. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized non-classical mechanism of aldosterone action in the heart and highlight LPAR2 as a promising therapeutic target for aldosterone-driven cardiovascular disease.

papers.title: Inverse relationship between mitochondrial and non-coding nuclear DNA content in free-living kinetoplastids
papers.abstract: The evolution of genome size and eukaryotic genome organisation has puzzled evolutionary biologists for decades. Are differences in DNA content and protein-coding capacity of eukaryotic genomes a result of natural selection, or neutral processes? If they were shaped by natural selection, which features might be connected with these differences: cell volume, ecological strategy, availability of nutrients, etc.? Kinetoplastids are protists with compact nuclear genomes that almost entirely lack introns, but whose mitochondrial DNA content (kDNA) can rival that of their nuclei. We hypothesised that the reduction in non-protein coding nuclear DNA content during the evolution of kinetoplastids is connected with an increase in kDNA content: species with larger fractions of total cellular DNA that is allocated to kDNA will have concomitantly smaller fractions of non-coding DNA in the nuclear genome. We developed a framework for estimation of DNA content in both the mitochondria and nuclei from quantitative fluorescence microscopy data, and inferred the fraction of non-coding DNA in nuclear genomes based on the combination of transcriptomic and fluorescence imaging data. Across 10 genetically distant isolates from diverse free-living kinetoplastid lineages, there is indeed a trend towards a lower proportion of non-protein-coding nuclear DNA when kDNA proportion is higher relative to the total DNA in the cell. This observation is consistent with the hypothesis that in free-living kinetoplastids, mitochondrial and nuclear genomes might co-evolve in terms of their DNA content. This finding raises the possibility that natural selection acts on genome size evolution in kinetoplastids, and contributes evidence and methodology to address this question more broadly in eukaryotes.

papers.title: Integrating single-cell and bulk transcriptomes identifies neuronal heat-stress-associated candidate genes in a reef-building coral
papers.abstract: Cell-type-specific molecular responses are obscured in bulk RNA sequencing, whereas generating matched single-cell datasets across environmental conditions remains costly and technically challenging, particularly in non-model organisms. Here, we present a workflow that integrates existing bulk and single-cell RNA-seq resources to prioritize cell-type-associated environmental-response genes. We demonstrate the workflow by examining heat-stress-associated neuronal genes in the reef-building coral Stylophora pistillata. Neuronal genes were first identified based on cell type-specific expression in single-cell transcriptomic data and then intersected with differentially expressed genes from bulk RNA-seq datasets under heat-stress. In parallel, we applied a deconvolution approach to infer cell type-specific expression changes directly from bulk data, independently capturing neuronal transcriptional responses. This integrated pipeline reduced thousands of heat-responsive genes previously identified in bulk RNA-seq studies to nine heat-associated, neuron-enriched candidates. Eight of the nine candidates showed their highest mean expression in the same neuronal subcluster. Targeted sequence-based characterization supported the identification of a TRPA-family ion channel, two calmodulin/centrin-family Ca2+-binding proteins, and a Class A/rhodopsin-like GPCR of unresolved ligand specificity. Two additional candidates were predicted secreted proteins belonging to conserved coral protein families, while the molecular functions of the remaining candidates remained unresolved. Their coordinated regulation suggests heat-associated remodeling of neuronal sensory and intracellular signaling processes. Our workflow provides a scalable framework for extracting cell type-associated molecular responses from existing transcriptomic resources and prioritizing candidates for further investigation. More broadly, it offers a generalizable strategy for investigating cell type-specific gene expression responses across organisms, cell types, and environmental conditions without requiring new single-cell datasets.

papers.title: Adaptive gene duplication can exceed optimal dosage
papers.abstract: Gene duplication is an important evolutionary mechanism contributing to genomic innovation and adaptation. While the long term fate of duplicated genes has been extensively studied, immediate effects such as those resulting from increase in gene dosage remain understudied. Of particular interest is the question of how expression level relates to the optimum after a duplication, as it could fall short, exceed or directly reach the optimal expression. In this study, we investigated the relationship between expression and fitness for 11 genes previously reported to increase fitness when duplicated in Saccharomyces cerevisiae to compare the expression level achieved by duplication to the one maximizing fitness. While most of the studied genes show little fitness variation across the expression levels tested, we found that ESP1, which encodes a separase essential to anaphase initiation, exhibits a clear fitness optimum at an expression level above the native single-copy state. However, the expression level associated with gene duplication exceeds the optimum. We find that ESP1 overexpression is associated with a reduced cell size and a lower proportion of the cell cycle spent in G2 phase, consistent with its role in cell cycle progression. We propose that the duplication of ESP1 accelerates the cell cycle, resulting in smaller, faster-dividing cells. When measured in different environments, the fitness functions also exhibit similar shapes, with slight variation in the optimal expression. Our findings highlight how gene duplication can confer an immediate selective advantage through dosage increase while being non-optimal, reversing the directionality of natural selection on expression level after duplication.

papers.title: Warming and biotic interactions shape selection on plant traits and their plasticity
papers.abstract: Global warming will impact natural selection on plant traits and their plasticity by influencing phenotypes, biotic interactions, and fitness. Because warming affects biotic interactions, community composition may influence how warming affects selection on plants, but this is little studied. We grew full-sibling pairs of Brassica rapa plants in an ambient and hot temperature environment and exposed them to visitation by a pollinator (Bombus terrestris), a pollinating herbivore (Pieris rapae), or their combination. We recorded plant phenotypes, insect visitation, herbivory, and plant fitness. We used these to calculated phenotypic selection on plant traits and their plasticity, including additive and nonadditive effects. Elevated temperature changed selection on traits related to pollinator attraction, such as flower number, nectar production, and floral scent emission. We found both positive and negative selection on temperature-mediated trait plasticity depending on the biotic treatment. Elevated temperature changed patterns of additive and non-additive selection on a variety of traits including flower morphology and scent. This study shows that elevated temperatures can reshape patterns of phenotypic selection, including nonadditive effects, and plastic trait expression. Effects of elevated temperature on phenotypic selection depended on the biotic interactors, highlighting the importance of community context for the effects of warming on natural selection.

papers.title: Bayesian inference of global land plant diversification dynamics across the Phanerozoic
papers.abstract: Underlying diversification patterns and potential drivers of land plants remain puzzling, particularly at deep-time and global scales. Here, we reconstruct the diversification dynamics of land plants using an updated time-calibrated phylogeny comprising approximately 30,000 extant species, and nearly 40,000 fossil occurrences within the Bayesian birth-death frameworks. Our analyses indicate that angiosperms exhibit the highest diversification rates, whereas ferns underwent a marked diversification increase during the Cretaceous, coincident with the rapid radiation of angiosperms. Among the major Phanerozoic mass extinctions, the Cretaceous-Paleogene event has the most significant impact on land plant diversity, with estimated genus-level losses of 13%, 14%, and 4% in bryophytes, pteridophytes, and gymnosperms. We identify a pattern consistent with competitive displacement scenario, in which pteridophytes origination rates declined as gymnosperm diversity increased, accompanying the transition from pteridophyte- to gymnosperm-dominated floras. We find that plant-insect interactions have originated as early as the emergence of pteridophytes, potentially promoting the diversification of pteridophytes and gymnosperms. During the Cretaceous, these associations shifted toward angiosperms, as indicated by a positive relationship between insect diversity and angiosperm origination rates. Finally, continental fragmentation, fluctuations in aridity, atmospheric carbon and sedimentary dynamics, showed stronger associations with the successive rise and decline of major land plant groups.

papers.title: Evolutionary constraint predicts the repeatability of transcriptional divergence during repeated adaptation
papers.abstract: The repeated evolution of similar phenotypes in response to shared ecological pressures provides striking examples of natural selection and raises broader questions about the predictability of evolution. Evolutionary constraint may shape this predictability, while the apparent extent of parallelism may also depend on the biological scale at which it is measured. When are adaptive solutions channeled along the same route? We addressed this question using three sympatric benthic-limnetic ecotype pairs of threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus), characterizing gene expression in gill and liver from wild-caught fish. We tested whether proxies of pleiotropic and coding-sequence constraint predicted the repeatability of transcriptional divergence across lakes. At the gene level, differential expression was strongly biased toward parallel rather than antiparallel responses. At the functional level, numerous pathways showed parallel enrichment, but the conservation of their underlying member-gene responses varied substantially, indicating that similar functional outcomes can arise with differing degrees of gene-level concordance. Most importantly, several proxies of evolutionary constraint predicted transcriptional repeatability, particularly in gill: broadly expressed, highly connected, and more slowly evolving genes showed more stable expression responses across lakes, with similar relationships evident for repeated use of genes within functionally parallel pathways. Together, these results show that both gene-level constraint and biological scale contribute to variation in molecular repeatability and suggest that the predictability of repeated adaptation may reflect an interaction between genetic architecture, population-genetic context, and the level of biological organization at which parallelism emerges.

papers.title: Generalized Maternal-Paternal Genotype Markov Model for Single-Cell Lineages
papers.abstract: Single-cell sequencing provides a rich source of data that can be used to model and estimate the evolution of somatic cells within individuals. Many common models for modeling DNA evolution in phylogenetics are based on continuous-time Markov processes that operate on aligned sites. For haploid DNA, such as found in mitochondria, there are many well established models for these processes but since nuclear DNA is diploid, containing copies of both the maternal and paternal genome, it is natural to develop continuous-time Markov processes adapted to diploid DNA. One possible model is that both the maternal and paternal evolve independently according to haploid models so that, in principle, DNA comes with a phase. i.e. a label that tells if the site was derived from the maternal or paternal sequence. However, this information may not be available in practice and only an unphased diploid genotype is available. That is, an unphased model groups both of the possible maternal-paternal labels into a single state. This grouping process, called ``lumping'', is used by other methods as well and results in a coarser process. Care must be taken so that the coarser process can still be modeled as a continuous-time Markov chain; the lumped process of the original phased Markov chain may or may not be Markovian, depending on restrictions imposed on the generator matrix. Here, we explore the mathematical formulations of phased and unphased Markov processes, as well as a collection of other diploid DNA models from the literature.

papers.title: A naturally evolved mutation in cavefish mc3r reshapes energy homeostasis across development in a nutrient-limited environment.
papers.abstract: Food availability in natural habitats is often unpredictable and drives the selection of adaptive strategies in organisms to survive food scarcity. However, the genetic and molecular mechanisms that enable animals to survive under such nutritional extremes are poorly understood. Naturally adapted organisms therefore provide powerful genetic systems for uncovering the mechanisms that maintain energy homeostasis under nutritional extremes. Here, we leveraged the cavefish Astyanax mexicanus to identify a naturally occurring Thr166Met missense mutation in the melanocortin 3 receptor (mc3r) that reprograms energy homeostasis to facilitate adaptation to nutrient deprivation. To determine its functional consequences, we introduced the mutation into zebrafish mc3r using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing. We show that adult mc3r mutants exhibit increased body size, adiposity, and hyperglycemia relative to wild-type animals, recapitulating key metabolic features of Tinaja cavefish and identifying mc3r as the first causal gene behind cavefish hyperglycemia. Investigations for early developmental consequences of the mutation revealed accelerated yolk utilization in mutant zebrafish larvae and strikingly elevated metabolic rates relative to WT, thus, uncovering a previously unrecognized role for mc3r in regulating energy expenditure. Importantly, the phenotype was also observed in Tinaja cavefish revealing a novel cavefish phenotype and establishing causal role for mc3r in elevated metabolic rate phenotype of cavefish. Together, these findings reveal that the Thr166Met variant produces distinct physiological consequences across life stages, enhanced energy storage and hyperglycemia in adulthood despite elevated larval energy expenditure. We propose that increased larval metabolism may support the energetic demands of enhanced foraging, whereas increased adiposity and blood glucose later in life provide energy reserves during periods of nutrient scarcity. More broadly, our study demonstrates how a single naturally evolved coding variant can reshape energy homeostasis across development and contribute to adaptation to nutrient-poor environments.

papers.title: Parallel differentiation extends beyond chromosomal inversions to small genomic islands on a background of rampant gene flow in the European flat oyster (Ostrea edulis)
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous genomic landscapes of differentiation can reveal evolutionary processes acting over different timescales. Whereas genetic structure in the European flat oyster, Ostrea edulis, is mainly shaped by geography, previous work suggested parallel differentiation between western and eastern Mediterranean populations and between Atlantic and North Sea populations, resulting in genetic convergence between range margin populations in some genomic regions. Here, we analyzed 27 oysters from four locations using moderate-coverage (~20X) short-read whole-genome sequencing. We first examined three known chromosomal inversions and found evidence that they predate divergence with the sister species O. chilensis. We then scanned the genome for parallel differentiation at the individual-SNP rather than sliding-window scale using the product of allele-frequency differences across the two geographic contrasts. Two of the three inversions were detected, but we also identified 12 small non-inverted genomic regions showing even stronger signals of parallel differentiation. These 'islands of parallelism' typically overlap one or a few genes, and most showed elevated dXY consistent with long-term barriers to gene flow. Two islands overlap nuclear ATP synthase subunits, while mitochondrial ATP8 shows a convergent amino-acid change, suggesting possible nuclear-nuclear and mitonuclear incompatibilities. Finally, demographic inference with heterogeneous gene flow supported post-glacial secondary contact and a lineage-based rather than geography-based population topology. Our results suggest that the genomes of O. edulis lineages have been largely porous to gene flow upon secondary contact, except for chromosomal inversions and small genomic islands. These regions likely act as barrier loci, preserving a signal of a shared evolutionary history among marginal populations that has otherwise been erased by rampant gene flow.

papers.title: Experimental evolution reveals competing selective forces during an early pollinator shift in monkeyflowers
papers.abstract: Understanding how complex multi-trait adaptations arise in nature remains a fundamental challenge in evolutionary biology. A classic example of this adaptation is the pollination syndrome, where integrated suites of floral characteristics co-evolve to attract specific pollinators. While transitions between pollination syndromes occur frequently, the underlying evolutionary trajectories traversed by adapting populations remain largely opaque. Here, we used an experimental evolution approach to track real-time phenotypic and genomic changes during a pollinator switch, leveraging the novel attraction to bumblebees exhibited by hybrids between the hummingbird-pollinated Mimulus cardinalis and the self-pollinating M. parishii. Within only three generations of bumblebee selection, we observed remarkably rapid shifts in floral traits, genotypes, and fitness. Our findings demonstrate that pollinator shifts are likely shaped by a complex interplay of selection, genomic conflict, and pleiotropic constraints that cannot be predicted simply by the genetic architecture of floral traits alone.

papers.title: Panic at the Discordance: the Asparagaceae Phylogenetic Backbone
papers.abstract: The Asparagaceae is an economically and ecologically important angiosperm (monocot) clade, containing iconic garden plants such as asparagus, hyacinth and agave, and arid-adapted keystone species like Joshua tree and dragon blood tree. The approximately 2,500 species in the family are spread across seven subfamilies: Agavoideae, Aphyllanthoideae, Asparagoideae, Brodiaeoideae, Lomandroideae, Nolinoideae and Scilloideae. Relationships among the seven subfamilies are generally unresolved and the sources of gene tree-species tree discordance are largely unknown. Investigating the biology underlying such discordance requires a robust sampling of both taxa and molecular markers, due to the extremely short branches that form the backbone of the Asparagaceae phylogeny. Using targeted sequencing of 1,726 low-copy nuclear genes, and a nearly complete sampling of genera, we interrogate relationships among all seven Asparagaceae subfamilies and investigate the underlying sources of discordance across the phylogeny. Analyses using different phylogenomic approaches (multispecies coalescence vs. nuclear gene supermatrix vs. chloroplast gene supermatrix) each revealed extensive discordance across the Asparagaceae backbone, which may be associated with rapid lineage diversifications that occurred in Africa shortly following the origin of the family ~49 Ma. Specifically, we found that two branches, representing ancestors of Aphyllanthoideae and Nolinoideae, may be responsible for much of the backbone discordance. The placement of Aphyllanthoideae, represented by one extant taxon (Aphyllanthes monspeliensis), is controversial with discordant topologies across many studies. However, multispecies coalescence-based analyses from this study strongly support a sister relationship between Aphyllanthoideae and a larger Agavoideae + Scilloideae + Brodiaeoideae clade. According to gene tree quartet frequencies and ABBA-BABA tests, we cannot reject incomplete lineage sorting (ILS) as the main source of discordance for the placement of Aphyllanthoideae; our results leave open the possibility of an ancient reticulation involving an ancestor of Aphyllanthoideae and an extinct basal Asparagaceae lineage. Regarding Nolinoideae, we found that conflicting support for two possible bifurcating clades (Asparagoideae + Nolinoideae vs. Asparagoideae + Lomandroideae) was associated with skewed support for alternative gene tree topologies, suggesting that phenomena other than ILS may explain the observed discordance. A quartet-based ABBA-BABA analysis, used to test for signatures of introgression, revealed a putative ancient hybridization event between two divergent, ancestral lineages which may have contributed to the origin of the Nolinoideae clade in Africa ~45 Ma. In sum, this study elucidates the long-troublesome backbone of the Asparagaceae phylogeny and advances our understanding of the evolutionary and biogeographical origins of all extant subfamilies. More broadly, this study expands our understanding of the various sources of gene tree discordance that may arise from natural processes associated with rapid lineage radiations across the tree of life.

papers.title: Canalization masks high levels of cryptic epigenetic and transcriptional plasticity in butterflies
authors: K. R. L. van der Burg
papers.abstract: Phenotypic plasticity is a common adaptation to heterogeneous environments. While it is well documented that trait plasticity can rapidly evolve, little is known about the developmental mechanisms that underlie variation in plasticity. Here, we compare diverged populations of the common buckeye butterfly (Junonia coenia): one population with canalized wing patterns that are insensitive to environmental conditions and another population that has distinctive seasonal color patterns. In common garden trials we were surprised to find dramatically elevated levels of transcriptional and chromatin accessibility plasticity during wing development of the canalized population compared to the seasonally plastic population. Further, using machine learning analysis of accessible chromatin sequences, we observed a broad heterochronic shift in motifs enriched in plastic putative regulatory elements to earlier stages of development in the canalized population, which we speculate may cause phenotype-related gene expression to move outside a wing color critical period. Together, our data lead us to propose a model where cryptic genetic processes are masked by a shift in chromatin remodeling, which in turn could produce a capacitor-like effect to maintain developmental genetic variation in the canalized population.

papers.title: The uplift of the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau reshaped genome architecture and diversification of Asian torrent catfishes
papers.abstract: Tectonic uplift and mountain building are major drivers of species diversification and adaptation, yet how they reshape genome architecture and promote evolutionary innovation remains poorly understood. Here, we generated multiple chromosome-level genomes for Asian torrent catfishes (Sisoridae) and performed phylogenomic and comparative genomic analyses. Our results support an Asian origin of Sisoridae and provide a refined phylogenetic topology for catfishes. Comparative analyses revealed extensive chromosomal rearrangements during sisorid evolution, indicating highly dynamic genome architectures. The timing of sisorid diversification overlaps with major phases of regional tectonic change, and analyses of phylogenetic discordance indicate heterogeneous contributions from incomplete lineage sorting and introgression. Elevational distribution was associated with variation in estimated molecular evolutionary rates, while exploratory scans identified lineage-specific candidates for selection and convergent evolution. Candidate coding and non-coding changes occur near genes with known roles in fin development, body patterning, and liver biology, but their effects on sisorid traits remain to be tested. Together, our results demonstrate how tectonic uplift reshaped genome architecture and diversification in Asian torrent catfishes and provide new insights into the genomic basis of adaptation in mountainous freshwater ecosystems.

papers.title: Connectivity, genetic diversity and adaptive potential of an endangered beetle: genomic evidence for veteran tree management
papers.abstract: Habitat fragmentation and destruction in old-growth forests represents a primary threat to specialist species, frequently resulting in the erosion of genetic diversity. The Hermit Beetle, Osmoderma barnabita, is a protected relic of primeval forests and an obligate saproxylic specialist whose larval development depends exclusively on the wood-mould of hollow trees. This study provides the first high-resolution, genome-wide assessment of O. barnabita across seven Polish forest complexes using double-digestion Restriction-site Associated DNA sequencing data from 49 individuals. Following rigorous quality control and reference bias assessment, we evaluate contemporary population structure. To distinguish between evolutionary processes, we isolated 2,920 putatively adaptive outliers from the neutral background, evaluating both neutral and adaptive genomic signals. The analyses revealed four distinct genetic clusters, confirming that the Polish metapopulation is severely subdivided. Crucially, the westernmost population in the Lower Silesian Forest emerged as the most divergent evolutionary unit (FST up to 0.360), suggesting potential hybrid origin or long-term isolation. We observed a striking linear correlation (R2=0.986) between neutral diversity and adaptive potential, indicating that genetic drift in small and isolated forest fragments is actively depleting the variation required for long-term persistence of this species. Our findings demonstrate significant gene flow restriction across all sites, suggesting that current conservation frameworks fail to encompass these highly differentiated lineages. To mitigate this genetic vulnerability, we recommend reclassifying these clusters as independent Management Units and Evolutionary Significant Units. Maintaining forest continuity and protecting local micro-habitats are essential to prevent further isolation and preserve the genomic integrity of this saproxylic flagship species.

papers.title: Multiple host species maintain genetic diversity in herbivore populations
papers.abstract: How natural populations maintain genetic variation for fitness remains a central problem in evolutionary biology. Theory predicts that opposing selective pressures across environments can preserve fitness-associated polymorphism, but how interactions among species contribute to this process remains poorly understood. Here we show that host diversity preserves standing genetic variation within sexual populations of the leafmining fly Scaptomyza flava. We evolved twelve populations for ten generations on either of two naturally co-occurring host plants or on both, pooling survivors from the two hosts before mating. Single-host populations evolved reciprocal fitness trade-offs, whereas two-host populations maintained relatively even performance across hosts. Whole-genome time series dynamics identified a linked region in which alleles increased on one host and decreased on the other, while showing little net change under two-host conditions. Wild flies reared from the two hosts showed corresponding allele-frequency differences within this region. Across the genome, two-host populations retained more rare variants than populations evolving on either host alone. These findings show that selection imposed by different host species in sympatry can maintain standing genetic diversity within an herbivore population.

papers.title: Heterogeneous evolution of effective recombination landscapes across percomorph fishes
papers.abstract: Recombination shapes allelic combinations across the genome and plays a central role in adaptation and speciation. While recombination rates are known to vary and evolve, how recombination landscapes diverge between populations and which processes drive this divergence remains poorly understood. Here, we use the Population Recombination Divergence Index (PRDI) to quantify divergence in effective recombination landscapes between seven pairs of populations and species from four percomorph fish lineages (cichlids, sticklebacks, killifish, and clownfish). While accounting for stochasticity and confounders of linkage disequilibrium (LD) -based recombination rate estimates, we find that recombination landscapes diverged substantially in all comparisons. This divergence generally increases with genetic differentiation and divergence time, but the amount of PRDI accumulated per unit of genetic divergence (FST), net nucleotide divergence (da), or divergence time varies markedly among population and species pairs. Comparisons across systems suggest that PRDI accumulation tends to be faster (per unit of FST, da, or divergence time) in pairs with higher inferred gene flow. We also introduce a local version of PRDI (_l) to better characterize genomic heterogeneity in effective recombination divergence. We find that higher inferred gene flow between populations tends to be associated with stronger intragenomic correlation between local FST and _l. Finally, we propose a conceptual framework for investigating how divergent selection and gene flow may interact to shape effective recombination landscape divergence. Our work highlights the heterogeneous dynamics of effective recombination landscape evolution, and motivates further theoretical and empirical efforts to integrate recombination landscape evolution into studies of adaptation and speciation.

papers.title: The molecular basis of hard cornification in the keratinized jaw sheaths and keratodonts of anuran tadpoles
papers.abstract: Hard cornification is the developmental process that produces the hardened epidermal structures that characterize tetrapod diversity, including scales, feathers, hair, and claws. This process relies on keratin proteins and additional reinforcing proteins that assemble, cross-link, and strengthen tissues to become mechanically resilient. Although the molecular composition of hard cornified tissues is known to vary among tetrapods, the program is least understood in amphibians. Within frogs, hard cornification occurs in the mouthparts of most tadpoles and in the nuptial pads, hindfoot claws, and foot tubercles of some adults. We characterized transcriptomic profiles of Bombina orientalis tadpoles at three developmental stages before, during, and after mouthpart cornification. We identified 25 keratin genes orthologous to amniote hard keratins in the B. bombina genome, 18 of which are upregulated in cornifying larval mouthparts. Furthermore, two of these hard keratin paralogs and an amphibian epidermal differentiation gene exhibit distinct spatial expression patterns within the jaw sheaths and keratodonts evidenced by in situ hybridization, suggesting they have discrete functional roles. The newly discovered diversity of the hard keratin repertoire in Bombina , and the concurrent expression of many of these paralogs in tadpole mouthparts, suggests that anuran hard cornification is much more complex than adult cornified traits thus far characterized in Xenopus frogs. Our results also challenge the notion that the diversification of keratins in Amphibia is primarily associated with the transition to more terrestrial habits, and may instead be shaped, in part, by the novel feeding apparatus of aquatic tadpoles.

papers.title: Partitioning covariance into causal and spurious components
papers.abstract: Statistical associations between two variables can arise via various causal mechanisms. For example, one variable may influence the other, or they may share common causes. Surprisingly little attention has been devoted to quantifying how such causal pathways contribute to the overall association between variables. Here, I present two methods for partitioning a covariance between variables X and Z into a causal component arising from the effect of X and Z and a spurious component arising via other pathways. Both methods rely on averaging causal decompositions over the distributions of the variables, but the decomposition and averaging are performed in different ways. The 'gradient' definition decomposes causal effects in the neighbourhood of naturally occurring values, making it relatively straightforward to estimate. It assumes that the cause variable X is normally distributed. In contrast, the 'two step' definition decomposes large ('step-wise') changes in values and makes no distributional assumptions. I describe applications of these methods to analysing natural selection and illustrate them using the covariance between body size and the number of eggs carried by pregnant male dusky pipefish, Syngnathus floridae. I partition this total covariance into a causal component due to the effect of body size on egg number and a spurious component arising from variation in body size and egg number among collection sites.

papers.title: Blackcaps (Sylvia atricapilla) with blood parasites have impaired oxidative status during autumn migration
papers.abstract: Parasites decrease host fitness, more so during physiologically challenging life stages such as migration. However, parasites are unevenly distributed among individuals, and hosts with different physiological condition may face different costs of migration with infections. We tested whether the relationship between infection by haemosporidian parasites and oxidative balance during autumn migration in blackcaps depends on individual age and sex, two major sources of variation in prevalence and physiological condition. We captured blackcaps at stopover in central Spain and measured infection status and physiological parameters. Blackcaps physiologically more prepared to depart from stopover had lower antioxidant capacity of plasma, probably because of physiological adjustments prior to the upcoming flight stage. Plasmodium parasites occurred only in coinfections, which were more frequent among young blackcaps. Regardless of individual sex and age, coinfected birds had lower antioxidant capacity of plasma, and blackcaps coinfected with Plasmodium had more oxidative damage to lipids in their red blood cells. Our results support the idea that haemosporidian infections impair the oxidative balance of blackcaps during autumn migration, which could impair individual performance and ultimately fitness, with increased population impacts during the first year of life when a larger proportion of individuals migrate coinfected with harmful Plasmodium parasites.

papers.title: Cldn18 evolution reveals pleiotropic constraints in vertebrate stomach loss
papers.abstract: Understanding the origins of anatomical innovations is central to elucidate the evolution of phenotypic diversity, as novel body plans often underpin the colonization of new ecological niches. The stomach, with its acid-secreting glands, evolved in the gnathostome ancestor and has been lost repeatedly. Claudin 18 (CLDN18) is a tight-junction protein that preserves gastric epithelial integrity against extreme H gradients and, in mammals, also acts in the lung through alternative first-exon isoforms. This dual role suggests that pleiotropy may shape the fate of CLDN18 after stomach loss. Here, we provide a detailed analysis of CLDN18 evolution across jawed vertebrates. CLDN18 originated in the gnathostome ancestor and is expressed in the stomach of elasmobranchs. We found no evidence of the gene in chimaeras or lungfishes, two additional agastric lineages, extending the loss of cldn18a previously described in agastric teleosts. Exon 1 architecture indicates a tandem duplication in the Euteleostomi ancestor, whereas stomach- and lung-associated isoforms are partitioned in most tetrapods examined. Monotremes, although agastric, retain only the lung-associated exon 1, consistent with lung function sustaining selection on the locus. Together, these findings reveal a complex evolutionary history involving gene loss, alternative splicing, tissue-specific regulation, and secondary exon loss, highlighting how pleiotropy and regulatory partitioning shaped the evolution of epithelia in jawed vertebrates.

papers.title: Order invariance of fitness makes evolution predictable despite strong history-dependent effects
papers.abstract: Environmental change is ubiquitous in nature, yet understanding its effect on the predictability of evolution remains a challenge. Previous work in microbes has shown that growth and fitness in a particular environment can depend strongly on the environments encountered previously. If such history-dependent effects are large, then any sequence of environments must be thought of as unique, and even a modest number of environments could generate a combinatorially large number of evolutionary paths. This would make evolution in changing environments difficult to predict. Here, we use cycles of three environments, which is the smallest number of environments which allow for comparisons of different environmental orderings -- X [->] Y [->] Z [->] X vs X [->] Z [->] Y [->] X -- to empirically test how environmental order affects the fitness of S. cerevisiae mutants. We measured the fitness of ~900 adaptive mutants in distinct three-environment cycles, and find large history-dependent effects which cause fitness in individual environmental components to differ drastically across the two directions of the cycle. However, these effects tend to compensate for each other, resulting in similar overall fitness across the whole cycle. This is true even when we specifically conduct experimental evolution in both directions of the same three-environment cycle. Of the ~450 mutants we isolated, only a small number of strains showed higher fitness in the direction in which they evolved. By splitting the contribution of each environment on fitness into its effect on the current and next component, we show that the invariance of overall fitness to environment order emerges because the effect of an environment on the next component is largely independent of the identity of the subsequent component, and can be captured by an additive model. Despite this general pattern of compensation, we do find instances of non-additivity, some of which are partly due to history-dependent effects lasting beyond two growth components. Overall, these results suggest that despite large history-dependent effects, fitness across a sequence of environments can be surprisingly predictable.

papers.title: Harnessing historical collections to reconstruct the invasion history of Microstegium vimineum (Poaceae)
papers.abstract: The evolutionary processes underlying successful invasions are often difficult to disentangle. Historical collections provide a temporal perspective, offering great potential to reconstruct invasion histories and identify the processes driving invasions. Japanese stiltgrass (Microstegium vimineum) is an invasive C4 grass introduced to eastern North America over a century ago and now established in 31 USA states. To reconstruct its invasion history, we leveraged low-coverage whole-genome sequencing of 142 herbarium and 330 contemporary samples spanning the temporal and spatial extent of the North American invasion and the native range in Asia. We identified three independent introductions in the USA: an awnless form in the South and two independent introductions of awned forms in the North, with limited admixture among introductions across space and time. In both regions, we observed high genetic diversity in the earliest available collections despite demographic bottlenecks and identified several putative selective sweeps in or near flowering-time genes, suggesting rapid evolution in the introduced range. Our analyses support separate invasions in the USA, likely facilitated by standing genetic variation and selection, but provide little support for admixture playing a major role. Our study highlights the power of historical collections to uncover the processes and mechanisms underlying successful biological invasions.

papers.title: Overcoming data limitations in macrogenetics: assessing and accounting for spatial heterogeneity in sequence data
papers.abstract: At large scales, our ability to compare genetic diversity across species is often challenged by the difficulty of extracting range-wide sequence data from online databases. Using mitochondrial DNA from amphibians and reptiles spanning across six regions: Brazilian Atlantic Forest, Iberian Peninsula, northwestern Africa, Arabian Peninsula, Madagascar and Australian Monsoonal Tropics, we develop and implement a framework to overcome common limitations in macrogenetics. We compiled and manually curated a spatially explicit genetic dataset from public repositories, quantified the spatial representativeness of genetic sampling across species' ranges and developed a novel interpolation framework to estimate and map species-specific patterns of intraspecific genetic diversity (ISD) while accounting for heterogeneous spatial sampling. We estimated mean nucleotide diversity across species to produce regional maps for each genetic marker. Our final dataset comprised 182 amphibian and 239 reptile species, encompassing 184 genera from 54 families. Range representativeness of genetic sampling was generally high, despite some variation across study regions. Spatial patterns of ISD revealed geographic heterogeneity, and were consistent across the best-sampled mitochondrial markers. By combining automated and manual georeferencing, quantifying range representativeness, and accounting for bias in spatial interpolations, our pipeline is marker-agnostic and directly applicable to nuclear and genomic data as they become available.

papers.title: Genomic Consequences of Altered Flood Regimes: Gene Flow and Adaptation in a Threatened Floodplain Plant
papers.abstract: Floodplains are highly dynamic ecotones where species persistence depends on synchrony between natural flow regimes and life-history. Artificial river engineering has profoundly altered these systems by reducing the frequency and magnitude of spring floods while increasing the unpredictability of flood timing and intensity during summer. These hydrological changes have disrupted historical patterns of dispersal, growth, reproduction, and competitive success among floodplain specialists. Effective conservation in these ecosystems therefore requires understanding how human-altered flow regimes have reshaped floodplain specialists' demography, genetic diversity, genetic connectivity, functional variation, and adaptive potential. Here, we address this challenge in Boltonia decurrens, a federally threatened floodplain plant endemic to the Illinois River Valley, by integrating a chromosome-scale reference genome, whole-genome resequencing, and common-garden adaptive trait measurements from 424 individuals across 17 populations. Demographic analyses revealed a severe recent bottleneck and a subsequent rebound. Population structure was clinal with downstream-dominant gene flow, indicating that regional population connectivity predominates over longer-distance gene flow. A subset of populations showed elevated genetic isolation with increased inbreeding and homozygous deleterious burden, revealing a genomic cost of disrupted floodplain connectivity. Common-garden observations and GWAS showed extensive within-population phenotypic and genetic variation in flowering time, flowering stem height, and year of first flowering (1st vs. 2nd year), which are hypothesized to buffer populations and to be selectively maintained under human-altered flow regimes. Finally, landscape-genomic approaches detected a divergent haplotype block separating northern and southern populations, suggesting that adaptive divergence can persist even in a system shaped by recurrent disturbance and ongoing gene flow.

papers.title: What shapes intraspecific genetic diversity in amphibians and reptiles? A comparative macrogenetic study across six biogeographic regions
papers.abstract: Aim: Given that much of Earth's biodiversity is contained within species, inferring intraspecific genetic diversity and identifying its ecological correlates is essential for understanding evolutionary processes and informing conservation. Here, we investigate broad-scale variation in species-level mitochondrial genetic diversity and evaluate the relative importance of alternative ecological hypotheses proposed to explain it. Location: Brazilian Atlantic Forest, Iberian Peninsula, northwestern Africa, Arabian Peninsula, Madagascar and Australian Monsoonal Tropics. Taxon: Amphibians and reptiles Methods: We assembled a comprehensive dataset by integrating and manually curating mitochondrial sequences, occurrence records, environmental data and species traits from multiple open-access sources. We used multiple mitochondrial genes to estimate mean nucleotide diversity for each study species and quantified regional variation in genetic diversity. We then used random forests models to evaluate the relative importance of selected variables representing hypotheses related to water-energy availability, topography, historical climatic stability, land-cover characteristics, species geographic characteristics, life-history traits, evolutionary history and conservation status. Results: The final dataset comprised 247 amphibians and 295 reptiles, for which 43 and 52 explanatory variables were evaluated, respectively. Overall, the strongest support was found for hypotheses related to life-history traits, topographic heterogeneity and water-energy availability. In amphibians, higher genetic diversity was associated with smaller body size and greater environmental heterogeneity, particularly broader elevational and precipitation gradients. In reptiles, genetic diversity was primarily associated with life-history traits, with species of smaller body size and lower reproductive output exhibiting higher diversity. Long-term climatic stability showed comparatively little explanatory power for both taxa. Main conclusions: Our comprehensive study demonstrates that integrating extensive manual data curation with comparative macrogenetic analyses provides a robust framework for identifying broad-scale ecological correlates of mitochondrial genetic diversity. These findings improve our understanding of the factors associated with contemporary patterns of genetic diversity and provide a foundation for future conservation assessments in data-limited systems.

papers.title: The evolutionary interplay between self-fertilisation and sex allocation in flowering plants
papers.abstract: Flowering plants vary in sex allocation (resource division between male and female function) and in selfing rate. These traits should evolve together: selfing changes fitness returns from pollen and ovules, whereas sex allocation changes the pollen available for selfing and export. Yet most models allow only one trait to evolve, leaving their evolutionary feedback unresolved. Here we model the joint evolution of sex allocation, pollen export and maternal control of competition between self- and cross-pollen. We show that selfing and sex allocation strongly influence one another, as selection favours associations between sex allocation and mating-system traits. When maternal control is fixed to recover classical mass-action, evolution can lead to the stable coexistence of selfing hermaphrodites and males specialised in pollen export. This androdioecy persists because hermaphrodites cannot prevent fertilisation by males. When maternal control of pollen competition also evolves, we find that where a mixed-mating equilibrium exists, selection again favours the emergence of androdioecy. As hermaphrodites evolve to favour their own pollen, however, they progressively exclude pollen from males, driving them extinct. The population may then return to mixed mating and repeat the process, or evolve complete selfing. We discuss these results with reference to known variation in the mating and sexual systems of plants.
